newsitem.title: USA: Cuban system violates human rights - exiles.
newsitem.headline: Cuban system violates human rights - exiles.

text.p: Cuban exiles will present a report to the United Nations Human Rights Commission which for the first time alleges Cuba's political system itself is a violation of human rights, a leading exile group said on Monday.

"All the violations of human rights in Cuba take place because the system itself, in its institutional structure, denies the Cuban people their rights," said Francisco Hernandez, president of the Miami-based Cuban-American National Foundation (CANF), a hardline exile group.
Hernandez said the group's reports to the Human Rights Commission in years past had documented violations by individuals, but had not named the system as a violator.

The report was to be presented to the commission on Tuesday in Geneva by Luis Zuniga, a CANF member and former Cuban political prisoner who will speak as an official of the Nicaraguan delegation appointed by President Arnoldo Aleman.
"This is the strongest allegation against Cuba ever presented before the United Nations," Zuniga, director of CANF's human rights project, said by telephone from Geneva.

In a report titled "The Status of Human Rights in Cuba", CANF said Cuba operated as a political monopoly with no "state of equilibrium or independence" between the executive, legislative and judicial powers as exists in other nations.

The report said judicial power was "dependent and politicized," with judges appointed by the Ministry of Justice and the Communist Party. The penal code provided the government with legal recourse to repress internal political dissent, the report said.
"For the first time, we are challenging the institutional system of Fidel Castro's regime," Hernandez said. "The nature of the system is the violator."

Hernandez also said the group was sending a letter to Representative Dan Burton, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives oversight committee, asking him to consider looking into any "influence Castro may have tried to exert over the U.S. political process."

Hernandez cited a Friday New York Times story that said Jorge Cabrera, a convicted drug smuggler who contributed to President Bill Clinton's re-election effort, was asked for a campaign contribution by a prominent Democratic fund raiser in a Havana hotel.

The Times, citing congressional investigators, said Vivian Mannerud, a Cuban-American businesswoman, told Cabrera in Havana that in exchange for a contribution he would be invited to a fund-raising dinner in honour of Vice President Al Gore.

"Given both of those individuals' evident relationship with Cuban dictator Fidel Castro and his longstanding desire to have U.S. sanctions against his regime lifted, we wish to respectfully request whether you would consider expanding your Committee's probe into Castro's possible role in this scandal," Hernandez wrote.
